item.title: MRI Features of Endometrial Hyperplasia With and Without Atypia and Early-Stage Endometrioid Carcinoma.
item.description:
Journal of computer assisted tomography
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features of endometrial hyperplasia (EH) and stage IA endometrial endometrioid carcinoma (EEC), and to assess MRI findings for distinguishing EH from EEC and for differentiating endometrial hyperplasia without atypia (EHWA) from endometrial atypical hyperplasia (EAH). METHODS: A total of 304 patients were retrospectively reviewed, including 107 with histopathologically confirmed EH (45 EHWAs and 62 EAHs) and 197 with stage IA EEC, all of whom underwent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 3 months before hysterectomy or biopsy/dilation and curettage. MRI findings were compared across groups. RESULTS: The frequencies of small intralesional cysts on T2-weighted (21% vs. 5%) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (19% vs. 4%) images and intraluminal linear structures on T2-weighted (12% vs. 2%) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (23% vs. 5%) images were higher in EH than in stage IA EEC, respectively (P<0.01). Signal intensity ratios on T2-weighted (2.45±1.14 vs. 1.66±0.65) and fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (0.97±0.27 vs. 0.81±0.22) images, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values (1.29±0.34 vs. 0.84±0.18×10-3 mm2/s) were higher in EH than in stage IA EEC, respectively (P<0.01). When comparing EHWA and EAH, the frequencies of small intralesional cysts on T2-weighted images (31% vs. 13%) and ADC values (1.38±0.34 vs. 1.22±0.33×10-3 mm2/s) were higher in EHWA than in EAH, respectively (P<0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Several MRI features, particularly ADC values, T2-weighted signal characteristics, small intralesional cysts, and intraluminal linear structures, may aid differentiation of EH from stage IA EEC. Discrimination between EHWA and EAH was modest and requires validation.

item.title: Basal forebrain atrophy links short-latency afferent inhibition to cognition in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease is closely associated with degeneration of the cholinergic system, yet the precise structure-function relationships underlying this link remain incompletely characterized. Short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI) is a widely used neurophysiological marker of cholinergic circuit integrity, but its specific anatomical substrate and relationship to domain-specific cognitive decline are not fully elucidated. This study integrated neurophysiology, structural MRI and cognitive data to characterize the association between cholinergic basal forebrain (cBF) atrophy, SAI and cognitive performance in Parkinson's disease. In this cross-sectional study, we enrolled 119 patients with Parkinson's disease spanning the cognitive continuum from normal cognition to dementia (mean age 63.9 ± 9 years) and 32 healthy controls. All participants underwent assessment of SAI and multimodal MRI for automated volumetry of anterior and posterior basal forebrain subregions and substantia nigra free-water mapping. Cognitive status was classified using the Parkinson's Disease Cognitive Rating Scale (PD-CRS), yielding scores for global cognition and fronto-subcortical and posterior-cortical functions. Regression models and bootstrap mediation analysis were used to examine the SAI-cognition association and decompose it into components shared with and independent of the cBF volume. SAI was reduced in patients compared with controls. Within the PD group, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates, SAI was significantly associated with PD-CRS total (β = -0.19, P = 0.013) and posterior-cortical scores (β = -0.44, P < 0.001), but not with the fronto-subcortical score (β = -0.13, P = 0.103). A mediation analysis identified a significant indirect path from SAI to global cognition through the posterior cBF volume [indirect β = -0.071, 95% confidence interval (CI) (-0.158, -0.013); 42% of the total association], with the residual direct path no longer statistically significant after inclusion of the mediator (β = -0.083, P = 0.260). A significant indirect path through the posterior cBF was additionally observed for the posterior-cortical score [indirect β = -0.061, 95% CI (-0.127, -0.006); 15% of the total association], alongside a substantial residual direct effect (β = -0.36, P < 0.001), consistent with SAI capturing aspects of the cholinergic system relevant to posterior-cortical performance beyond macroscopic cBF atrophy alone. These findings are consistent with SAI reflecting cholinergic circuit integrity linked to cBF structural status. The observed pattern of association, in which the posterior cBF volume captures a substantial proportion of the SAI-cognition covariance, positions SAI as a candidate functional marker for tracking cholinergic contributions to cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease, pending longitudinal validation.

item.title: Limbic circuit alterations in bipolar disorder.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
INTRODUCTION: This study investigated the spatial and temporal pattern of brain white matter (WM) alterations and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in bipolar disorder (BD). METHODS: Multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected from 67 BD patients (during manic, depressive, or euthymic phases) and 125 healthy controls (HC) at baseline, and from a subsample of 33 BD patients (in a different illness phase) and 23 HC after follow-up. Analyses of diffusion MRI and resting-state functional MRI were performed to characterise fixel-based metrics in WM and their relationship with intrinsic brain activity in BD and HC, as well as across timepoints. RESULTS: BD exhibited a spatial pattern of WM alterations characterised by reductions in fibre density and/or bundle cross-section involving fornix and cingulum (major limbic pathways), alongside portions of other tracts, compared with HC. Reduced fibre density in the fornix was associated with intrinsic activity changes involving midbrain, thalamus, and connected fronto-temporal cortical areas within the default-mode network in BD. These alterations showed no significant changes over time or across illness phases. CONCLUSIONS: These findings converge on limbic circuit alterations and suggest a relationship between structural abnormalities of the fornix and functional changes in intrinsic brain architecture in BD.

item.title: Reciprocal 16p11.2 Copy Number Variants Differentially Alter Regional Brain Anatomy and Allometric Scaling
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Reciprocal 16p11.2 copy-number variants (CNVs) confer substantial risk for neuropsychiatric disorders and produce opposing effects on brain size, with larger brain volume in deletion carriers and smaller volume in duplication carriers. Regional alterations broadly parallel this global phenotype, but because regional brain measures scale nonlinearly with brain size, it remains unclear whether regional differences reflect expected consequences of altered brain size, regional anatomy disproportionate to brain size, or fundamental alterations in allometric scaling. We analyzed 285 imaging sessions from 235 participants (49 deletion, 59 duplications, 127 controls) using log-log allometric models to distinguish these possibilities. Brain-size adjustment revealed widespread cortical disproportion in both CNVs, with predominantly reciprocal effects driven by surface area rather than cortical thickness, whereas subcortical structures showed convergent reductions disproportionate to brain size. Strikingly, examining genotype-specific scaling exponents revealed distinct allometric patterns between the CNVs. In duplication, regional differences predominantly reflected fixed shifts relative to brain size. In deletion, by contrast, regional differences more frequently varied with brain size, with substantial exponent deviations affecting 32% of disproportionate cortical regions compared with 12% in duplication. Thus, reciprocal 16p11.2 dosage does not simply shift regional anatomy in opposite directions: duplication largely preserves the normally conserved scaling of regional anatomy with brain size, whereas deletion more extensively disrupts it.

item.title: Functional and Neurotransmitter Organization of Cortical Gray Matter Remodeling During Pregnancy
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Pregnancy is a period of profound neuroplasticity, marked by widespread, spatially heterogeneous reductions in cortical gray matter volume (GMV). Yet, whether this remodeling affects cognition is unclear: subjective memory complaints are common during pregnancy, but objective findings are mixed. Using densely sampled longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) across pregnancy, we examined whether gestational GMV change corresponds spatially with normative maps of cognitive function and neurotransmitter receptors. We analyzed 19 T1-weighted MRI sessions of 1 healthy primiparous woman spanning preconception to 36 weeks gestational age. The GMV change map was annotated using 10 cognitive domain maps comprised of 115 Neurosynth terms and 16 positron emission tomography receptor and transporter maps from healthy adults, using dominance analysis and partial least squares (PLS) analysis with spin tests to account for spatial autocorrelation. Total cortical GMV declined by 4.24%. The 10 cognitive domains accounted for significant spatial variation in GMV change (R 2 adj = 0.16; spin P = .03), with learning and memory (37.7%) and action (27.3%) accounting for the largest shares of explained variance. PLS revealed a shared spatial axis in which learning and memory were associated with smaller GMV reductions while action was associated with greater reductions (spin P = .046). The receptor and transporter maps also accounted for significant spatial variation (R 2 adj = 0.22; spin P = .02). PLS identified a significant neurochemical pattern (spin P = .009), with greater GMV reductions in regions rich in cholinergic (VAChT) and noradrenergic (NET) markers and smaller reductions in regions rich in serotonergic, GABA A , and muscarinic M1 receptors. This receptor-derived pattern was positively associated with social function and negatively associated with action. Together, these findings provide new evidence that pregnancy-related GMV remodeling is organized along functional and neurotransmitter receptor axes, suggesting that maternal brain plasticity is a targeted process that may support selective cognitive adaptation.

item.title: Excitation/Inhibition Balance in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: A Functional MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance is implicated in the pathophysiology of psychosis, but the extent to which this is evident before the onset of illness is unclear. Here, we investigated E/I-related brain dynamics using the Hurst exponent (HE) derived from resting-state MRI in two longitudinal cohorts of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P): PSYSCAN (190 CHR-P individuals and 115 controls) and Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia (826 CHR-P individuals and 241 controls). Both cohorts showed lower whole-brain HE in CHR-P individuals than in controls at baseline, with the most prominent differences observed in the somatomotor network and thalamus. In both cohorts, normative receptor distributions significantly predicted the spatial pattern of HE differences, with consistent contributions from norepinephrine, serotonin, and opioid receptors. In PSYSCAN, 21 CHR-P individuals transitioned to psychosis during follow-up. There was preliminary evidence that subsequent transition to psychosis was associated with a longitudinal reduction in HE in the right inferior parietal cortex and that baseline regional HE showed above-chance prediction of subsequent transition at the individual level. Together, these findings suggest that vulnerability to psychosis is associated with reduced HE, consistent with less persistent brain dynamics and increased excitability.

item.title: Microstructural Analysis of Language Pathways' Development in Term Neonates
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding the early development of language pathways is essential for elucidating how neonatal brain organization supports the acquisition of linguistic skills. In this study, we investigated microstructural changes in term human neonates scanned at postmenstrual ages (PMA) of 37 to 44 weeks. Using diffusion MRI data from 310 healthy infants in the developing Human Connectome Project, we employed q-space diffeomorphic reconstruction to map major language tracts involved in language processing. Fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and other diffusion-based biomarkers were quantified in pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus, extreme capsule, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. Our results revealed significant weekly differences in microstructural integrity across these tracts, with particularly robust age-related reductions in mean and radial diffusivity. In addition, we observed leftward asymmetries in multiple language pathways, suggesting that hemispheric specialization emerges by this early postnatal stage. Although PMA at scan predicted the most pronounced shifts in diffusion metrics, sex showed minimal impact on developmental trajectories. These findings highlight the rapid and tract-specific organization of language-relevant connections during the first weeks of life, providing normative data against which atypical patterns can be evaluated. More broadly, this work offers new insights into the foundation of language circuitry in neonates, informing future studies of neurodevelopmental disorders and potential early-life interventions.

item.title: Connectomic Flow Across Cortical Sensory Systems in Juvenile Fibromyalgia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.

item.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

item.title: Socioeconomic disadvantage alters developmental patterning during fetal cortical maturation: evidence from structural covariance network analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with differences in child neurodevelopment that are detectable in utero. Existing fetal imaging work characterizes these differences in terms of tissue volumetry. However, fetal brain development also hinges on tightly regulated spatiotemporal patterning which, if disrupted, can alter long-term neurodevelopment. A cohort of 213 typically developing fetuses underwent fetal brain MRI between 20 and 38 gestational weeks. Cortical thickness was estimated across 78 regions and used to construct structural covariance networks within overlapping gestational windows. We used the Child Opportunity Index (3.0) as a measure of socioeconomic disadvantage. Population-wide development was characterized by significant gestational age-related decline in global density (β = −0.038, p = 0.002) and global synchrony (β = −0.022, p = 0.001). Nodal degree distribution broadened from leptokurtic to platykurtic, consistent with a transition from globally synchronized to segregated and localized growth. The Low COI group showed an attenuated decline (adj R² = 0.21) and a greater dispersion around the fitted model than the High COI group (adj R² = 0.54) in global density. Low COI fetuses showed delayed emergence of architectural hubs, spatially restricted to primary sensory and motor cortical regions alongside slower cortical thickness accrual in seven hub regions. Socioeconomic disadvantage is associated with the synchrony and spatial organization of cortical maturation in-utero.

item.title: Within-person ovarian hormone variation and structural connectome topology: a three-visit diffusion MRI study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Ovarian hormone variation has been associated with brain tissue measurements, but whether it accompanies changes in global structural network topology remains uncertain. We analysed 22 naturally cycling participants from OpenNeuro ds005360, with serum measurements and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging during menses, estimated ovulation and the mid-luteal phase. Longitudinal anatomical processing, anatomically constrained tractography and SIFT2 weighting yielded 66 connectomes with 84 nodes. Four primary mixed models tested within-person estradiol (E2) or progesterone (P4) associations with total-weight-normalized global efficiency and modularity Q, adjusting for participant-average hormone concentration, visit order and motion. No association survived four-test false-discovery-rate correction. The largest estimate was negative for E2–efficiency (standardized β = −0.132; 95% confidence interval − 0.258 to − 0.006; p = 0.0398; q = 0.159). Its participant-cluster bootstrap interval excluded zero, but permutation q = 0.111 also exceeded the corrected threshold. The negative direction persisted across participant omissions and alternative graph definitions, but 9 of 22 omissions gave p ≥ 0.05. Secondary global, nodal and connected-edge analyses yielded no corrected discovery. These findings provide no multiplicity-corrected evidence of a hormone association with the tested global topology measures. They do not establish structural invariance. The E2–efficiency direction warrants independent evaluation with larger samples and denser longitudinal measurements.

item.title: Quantitative Resting-State Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Reveals White Matter Network Reorganization in Older Adults With White Matter Hyperintensities
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background/Objectives: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are important imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease in older adults and are closely associated with cognitive decline. However, WMH burden alone cannot fully explain interindividual differences in cognitive impairment. This study constructed white matter resting-state functional networks based on the multimodal white matter atlas (MWMA) and investigated WMH-related alterations in network topology and their associations with cognitive function. Methods This single-center cross-sectional study included 171 older adults, comprising 50 participants with absent or mild white matter hyperintensities and 121 participants with moderate-to-severe white matter hyperintensities. All participants underwent three-dimensional T1-weighted imaging, T2-FLAIR imaging, and resting-state BOLD-fMRI. WMH grading and segmentation were performed using T2-FLAIR images. White matter network nodes were defined using the MWMA atlas, and 173 cerebral white matter regions of interest were retained. Individual 173 × 173 white matter functional connectivity matrices were constructed. Graph-theoretical metrics were calculated across a sparsity range of 0.05–0.50, and area under the curve values were used for statistical analysis. Group differences were assessed using general linear models adjusted for age, sex, years of education, and mean framewise displacement. Exploratory partial correlation analyses were performed in participants with complete cognitive data. Results Both groups retained small-world organization. Compared with controls, the WMH group showed increased aγ and aσ, whereas aEglob, aEloc, and aLp did not differ significantly. The WMH group also showed increased DMN-SMN inter-module connectivity, without significant intra-module differences. Nodal abnormalities were spatially heterogeneous: increased aBc was mainly located in WMH-affected regions, whereas abnormal aDc and aNe were more often distributed in normal-appearing white matter. Several abnormal nodal metrics were associated with TMT-A, TMT-B, and MoCA performance. Conclusions Moderate-to-severe WMH is associated with white matter functional network reorganization rather than complete topological breakdown. These alterations may contribute to WMH-related cognitive decline, particularly impairments in processing speed and executive function.

item.title: Probabilistic neural code for subjective value and metacognition in human cortex.
item.description:
Science advances
Subjective value underlies many everyday decisions, yet the neural representations supporting these valuations are inherently noisy and subject to uncertainty. Whether humans have metacognitive access to this uncertainty and how this access is supported neurally remain unclear. Here, we provide converging behavioral and neural evidence that subjective value is represented probabilistically in the human brain. Behaviorally, participants' uncertainty reports tracked trial-by-trial fluctuations in valuation. Neurally, we decoded probability distributions over value from functional magnetic resonance imaging activity in ventromedial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex, and superior parietal lobe and intraparietal sulcus. Decoded neural uncertainty predicted behaviorally reported uncertainty across trial, item, and individual levels. Moreover, predicting behavioral uncertainty required modeling the covariance structure of population noise. These findings indicate that neural populations jointly encode value and uncertainty, extending probabilistic population coding from perception, working memory to subjective value, and providing a neural basis for metacognitive access to uncertainty in value-based decisions.

item.title: Visual learning through auditory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep.
item.description:
Science advances
Visual learning, like other kinds of learning, has classically been attributed to intensive, active training; however, whether it can be achieved via effortless, passive reactivation remains unresolved. Here, we triggered targeted reactivation using auditory tones that had acquired contextual meaning through preceding visual-auditory associative learning. Re-exposure to learned tones improved subsequent visual performance during both wakefulness and slow-wave sleep. Wake reactivation matched training in both improvement and improvement per trial, whereas sleep reactivation surpassed both wake reactivation and training. By contrast, re-exposure to unlearned tones impaired performance only during slow-wave sleep. Reactivation-induced improvement and impairment were strictly orientation- and location-specific and were associated with a convergent auditory-visual coupling pathway. Beyond this shared pathway, auditory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep unfolded through distinct coupling architectures linking sensory and higher-order cortical regions. Collectively, our findings establish auditory reactivation as a highly efficient route to visual learning, identify sleep as its most potent state, and reveal a double-edged, state-dependent neuroplastic architecture.

item.title: Structural and resting-state functional brain alterations in male smokers: a combined voxel-based morphometry and functional connectivity analysis.
item.description:
Nicotine & tobacco research : official journal of the Society for Research on Nicotine and Tobacco
Introduction Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that chronic smoking is associated with gray matter volume (GMV) reductions and resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) abnormalities. However, these changes have largely been investigated independently, and the relationship between regional GMV alterations and corresponding rsFC changes remains poorly characterized. Integrating structural and functional metrics may enhance understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying nicotine dependence. Methods We recruited 51 male smokers and 52 age-matched healthy controls. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was performed to identify regions with significant GMV differences between groups. These regions were subsequently used as seeds for seed-based whole-brain rsFC analysis. Results Compared with controls, smokers exhibited significantly reduced GMV in the bilateral fusiform gyrus, left temporal pole (TP), and right inferior occipital gyrus. Smokers also showed enhanced rsFC within multiple circuits, including the left fusiform gyrus-right TP, left TP-left inferior frontal gyrus, and right fusiform gyrus-left rolandic operculum, whereas rsFC between the right fusiform gyrus and left insula was significantly decreased. Correlation analyses revealed that left TP GMV was negatively correlated with smoking duration and cumulative tobacco exposure (pack-years). Furthermore, rsFC strength between the left fusiform gyrus and right TP was negatively correlated with both the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND) and DSM-5 tobacco use disorder severity scores. Conclusions These findings suggest that chronic smoking is associated with concurrent GMV reductions and rsFC alterations within visual, social cognitive, and sensorimotor networks, with the left fusiform gyrus-right TP connectivity showing potential relevance to the severity of tobacco use disorder.

item.title: Resting-State Alpha Power and Cross-Hemispheric Beta Connectivity Are Associated With Individual Differences in Voice Identity Perception.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Human voices convey not only linguistic content but also rich information about speaker identity. Individual differences in voice discrimination are robust and trait-like, yet their neurophysiological substrates remain unclear. In the present study, we investigated whether resting-state electroencephalography (rsEEG) is associated with individual differences in voice identity perception, assessed using the Sisu Voice Matching Test (SVMT). Method A total of 61 native Mandarin speakers underwent eyes-open and eyes-closed rsEEG recordings, from which spectral power and interchannel coherence were extracted across eight canonical frequency bands. Behavioral performance on SVMT was examined alongside additional cognitive and perceptual measures, and principal component analysis was used to derive orthogonal covariates for specificity analyses, which enabled us to determine whether the rsEEG-SVMT relationships were independent of broader cognitive factors. Results Our results revealed distinct neural-behavioral associations across resting-state conditions: In eyes-open recordings, alpha-band power was positively associated with accuracy on telling-together trials, while cross-hemispheric beta-band coherence between right frontal and left temporo-parietal regions correlated with overall and pseudo-word performance. In contrast, eyes-closed spectral power showed limited explanatory value, with a specific negative beta coherence between left central and right posterior sites associated with poorer performance. Notably, the alpha power effect was attenuated after controlling for domain-general cognitive factors, whereas the beta coherence-SVMT associations remained robust, indicating greater specificity to voice identity processing. Conclusions These findings suggest that individual differences in voice discrimination are grounded in stable neural traits that are differentially expressed across background resting-state conditions. Specifically, they support a two-tier framework in which spectral power reflects domain-general cognitive readiness, whereas network-level beta-band connectivity constitutes a more selective neural signature of voice identity perception. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34914567.

item.title: The what, how and where of statistical learning: a neurocognitive synthesis.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
The ability to learn environmental regularities - statistical learning - is crucial for language, cognition and behaviour. Despite decades of research, fundamental questions remain about what statistical learning is, how the mind supports it and where in the brain it is implemented. We address these questions with a framework based on Marr's levels of analysis. At the 'what' level, we suggest that statistical learning is best defined in terms of its goal: to learn latent structure in the input across repeated exposures. We focus on three widely studied sequential statistical learning tasks that embody this definition: embedded pattern, artificial grammar and serial reaction time tasks. At the 'how' and 'where' levels, our comprehensive reviews reveal that sequential statistical learning depends on at least two cognitive learning processes (prediction-based learning and chunking) and two well-established neural learning circuits (rooted in the basal ganglia and the medial temporal lobe). We describe empirically motivated 'many-to-many' mappings between the tasks, learning processes and neural circuits that integrate the three levels. Further, we suggest that task, input and learner characteristics can shift the relative reliance on these processes and circuits. Overall, our synthesis elucidates the cognitive and neural substrates of sequential statistical learning and provides predictions to guide future research.

item.title: Biotin intake and mental health: findings from a large population-based cohort and biological insights from hippocampal and gut-brain pathways.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
The relationship between biotin and mental health remains largely unexplored. Leveraging data from the UK Biobank prospective cohort, we found that dietary biotin intake in the second quartile was associated with a 15% lower risk of major depressive disorder, while intake in the third quartile was associated with a 14% lower risk of anxiety disorder, compared with the lowest quartile. Furthermore, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses revealed nonlinear associations between dietary biotin intake and both outcomes, with the lowest risks of incidence observed at biotin intake levels of approximately 40-50 μg. Neuroimaging analyses further revealed positive associations between dietary biotin intake and fractional anisotropy in the cingulum-hippocampus tract, suggesting a potential link between biotin intake and white matter microstructure in a pathway involved in emotional regulation. We then examined the effects of a 9-week biotin intervention in mice and observed changes consistent with two potential pathways: a hippocampus-related pathway involving enhanced protein biotinylation, reduced neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) expression, and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression, and a gut-brain axis pathway characterized by greater microbial diversity and an increased relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, which was positively associated with brain 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) levels. These findings provide complementary biological evidence that may help explain the observed association between dietary biotin intake and mental health.

item.title: Insomnia reorganizes large-scale functional connectivity abnormalities in depression: Evidence from functional gradients and neurotransmitter mapping.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Sleep disorders are one of the most prevalent and clinically important features of depression, yet their impact on the large-scale organization of brain functional abnormalities remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether insomnia reshapes whole-brain resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) abnormalities in depression and alter their hierarchical and neurochemical organization. Resting-state fMRI data were acquired from depressed patients with (INS, n = 32) and without insomnia symptoms (NINS, n = 24), and healthy controls (HC, n = 45). Network-based statistics (NBS) was used to identify altered RSFC subnetworks. We then examined the hierarchical distribution of network abnormalities using the principal functional gradient, assessed clinical relevance, and evaluated their spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter atlas. Results showed that the INS group exhibited more widespread functional connectivity impairments, primarily concentrated in the visual and sensorimotor networks. Moreover, these abnormal connections showed a hierarchical distribution pattern along the principal functional gradient, with lower-level sensory systems more affected than higher-level cognitive networks. Significant differences in node degree were observed in the visual network, and functional connectivity within this network was associated with anxiety scores in the INS group. Spatial similarity analyses revealed overlapping but distinct neurotransmitter profiles across groups, with shared correlations for mGluR5 and stronger μ-opioid-related associations in the INS group. These findings suggest that insomnia symptoms in depression are associated not simply with more severe dysfunction, but with a reorganization of large-scale functional abnormalities toward lower-order sensory systems, characterized by a gradient-dependent connectivity distribution and altered associations with specific neurotransmitter systems, particularly μ-opioid receptors.

item.title: Linking Theory of Mind and Cardiac Vagal Regulation: the Integrative Role of the Posterior Cerebellum.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Interpersonal interactions are fundamentally regulated by Social Cognition, a multifaceted construct encompassing the cognitive and neural processes used to navigate the social environment. Within this overarching architecture, Theory of Mind (ToM), or mentalizing, provides a foundational dual-level framework of implicit and explicit systems. Although these functions traditionally rely on a cortical mentalizing network, recent findings support a cerebellar contribution to ToM processes. Given that the cerebellar computational architecture is suited for the rapid, automated processing of visual social cues, investigating lower-level social decoding offers a unique window into the cerebellar contribution to ToM. Building on this framework, the present research explored the relation between cerebellar morphometry and lower-level ToM in healthy subjects. Participants underwent MRI to assess cerebellar Gray Matter volumes and completed the computerized version of the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET). Since the lower-level mentalizing is closely tied to complex interactions between the Central and Autonomic Nervous Systems (ANS), the present study also examined the relationships between cerebellar volumes and Heart Rate Variability, namely the variations of Root Mean Square of Successive Differences (RMSSD) values across the RMET procedure. Findings revealed that volumes of cerebellar lobules VI, VIIb, Crus II, and vermis IX predicted the RMET accuracy. Furthermore, the volume of vermis IX selectively predicted RMSSD variation during the rest-recovery transition, with smaller vermis IX volumes associated with a sharper, more progressive RMSSD decline. Overall, these data highlight that posterior cerebellar morphometry is associated with RMET performance and cardiac vagal regulation, thus supporting lower-level mentalizing.

item.title: Neurocomputational Mechanisms Underlying Differential Framing Effects on Generosity and Honesty.
item.description:
NeuroImage
The framing effect, a robust cognitive bias, demonstrates that human decision-making is influenced by whether outcomes are presented as gains or losses. Nevertheless, substantial debate remains regarding the extent to which loss frames facilitate or inhibit prosocial behaviors, and the neurocognitive processes through which frames drive these divergent effects remain poorly understood. We combined behavioral analyses, computational modeling, and brain imaging to dissect the neurocognitive substrates underpinning framing effects on two distinct forms of prosociality: generosity and honesty. Fifty-three healthy adult participants completed both the Dictator Game (DG), which primarily captures generosity-related considerations, and the Message Game (MG), which involves honesty-related considerations, allowing us to examine how gain versus loss frames affect choices across these two prosocial decision contexts. Behavioral analyses revealed a significant game type × frame interaction, while computational modeling further identified opposite frame-related changes in the generosity-related parameter β and the honesty-related parameter δ, together revealing differential framing effects across prosocial domains. At the neural level, activations in the amygdala and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) were modulated by frame and game type: both regions showed greater activation for DG in the gain frame and MG in the loss frame than for DG in the loss frame and MG in the gain frame. Moreover, functional coupling between the vmPFC and temporoparietal junction (TPJ) exhibited an interaction effect consistent with the regional activation pattern, while amygdala and TPJ coupling showed a similar interaction trend. Collectively, these findings suggest the involvement of an amygdala-TPJ-vmPFC circuit in framing-related decision-making, with the TPJ potentially participating in interactions between affective and value-related processes that may contribute to differential framing effects on generosity and honesty.

item.title: Unraveling the interplay between sensory information and semantic architecture in brain concept representation: the role of abstraction.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Understanding how abstract and concrete words are represented in the brain requires disentangling the contribution of sensorimotor information from the organization of semantic knowledge. These dimensions, here referred to as abstractness and abstraction, respectively, are typically confounded, limiting our ability to identify their distinct neural correlates. The present study aimed to dissociate the roles of abstractness and abstraction in word processing by introducing superordinate words as a critical comparison category. Behavioral norming and feature production tasks were used to quantify sensory-related properties and semantic architecture, operationalized in terms of generalizability, feature relevance, and representational specificity. These measures informed computational models capturing abstractness, abstraction, sensorimotor content, and distributional similarity. Neural data were acquired using electroencephalography and analyzed with representational similarity analysis to assess model-brain correspondence over time. Behaviorally, superordinate words patterned with concrete words on sensory properties but with abstract words on measures of semantic architecture. In the electrophysiological data, concrete words elicited stronger negativities than both abstract and superordinate words in the N400 and N700 time windows, whereas the contrast between abstract and superordinate words did not reach significance. Representational similarity analysis revealed that, among the models tested, the abstraction model was significantly associated with the neural response patterns in the N400 and N700 latencies, whereas models based on abstractness, sensorimotor or distributional information did not reach the significance threshold. Within the participants and stimuli tested, these results indicate that semantic architecture provides a useful framework for understanding the neural dynamics of word processing, alongside sensorimotor grounding. They suggest that abstraction may play a central role in structuring conceptual representations, providing a unifying account that bridges embodied and formal theories of semantic representation.

item.title: Altered frontoparietal BOLD-CSF coupling in drug-naïve young adults with major depressive disorder: Links to neural variability, cognition, and GABAergic gene expression.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Glymphatic dysfunction, indexed non-invasively via BOLD-CSF coupling, a putative proxy for cerebrospinal fluid clearance, has been implicated in mood disorders, but its regional relationships with neural activity, network dynamics, cognition, and molecular features in major depressive disorder (MDD) remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state fMRI from 109 MDD patients and 106 healthy controls (HC), assessing BOLD-CSF coupling at global, network, and subnetwork levels and its associations with mfALFF, BOLD signal variability (SDBOLD), functional connectivity (FC), cognition, and Allen Human Brain Atlas transcriptomic profiles. MDD patients showed modestly reduced global BOLD-CSF coupling (p = 0.036), concentrated in higher-order networks (p = 0.013), including the default mode and frontoparietal networks (FPN, both p = 0.019). Coupling was negatively correlated with SDBOLD and FC across most networks (q < 0.05), and the coupling-FC relationship was selectively weaker within the FPN in MDD (q = 0.019), supported by a group-by-coupling interaction. Within the FPN, SDBOLD was associated with cognitive performance, and mediation analysis indicated an indirect pathway from FPN coupling to cognition via SDBOLD that was nominally significant in HC but not MDD, although the moderating effect of group was not itself significant. Transcriptomic analysis linked regional coupling alterations to gene expression (30.3% variance explained, p = 0.040) enriched for GABAergic signaling. These findings suggest that BOLD-CSF coupling alterations in MDD, concentrated in higher-order networks, are associated with altered neural variability, disrupted connectivity, and cognitive deficits, and spatially correspond with the cortical expression of genes enriched for receptor and channel functions.

item.title: Whole-brain mapping of TMS-induced discomfort with large-scale concurrent TMS-fMRI.
item.description:
Brain stimulation
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is widely used for causal brain mapping and neuromodulation therapies, yet TMS-induced discomfort remains a prevalent and under-characterized confound that may influence measured neural responses. This study aimed to characterize the whole-brain neural signatures of TMS-induced discomfort and quantify its contribution to TMS-evoked neural activity. A total of 165 participants, including healthy individuals (N = 80) and individuals with elevated depression and/or anxiety symptoms (N = 85), underwent concurrent TMS-fMRI across 11 cortical stimulation sites, yielding 1,535 runs. Following each run, participants rated TMS-induced discomfort using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS). Multivariate brain-discomfort associations were modeled using a principal component analysis and sparse canonical correlation analysis (PCA-sCCA) framework with cross-validation. TMS-induced discomfort varied systematically across stimulation sites, with greater discomfort reported for frontal and inferior regions. PCA-sCCA identified distributed neural signatures of TMS-induced discomfort spanning sensorimotor, attentional, limbic, and default mode networks, as well as subcortical regions. Neural signatures differed between healthy and symptomatic groups, demonstrating both shared and group-specific patterns. The discomfort-related activity comprised approximately 12% and 25% of TMS-evoked neural responses in healthy and symptomatic groups, respectively, with greater contributions observed at frontal stimulation sites. Accounting for the discomfort-related component altered estimates of TMS-evoked response magnitude and effect size. TMS-induced discomfort engages distributed brain-wide networks and constitutes a substantial component of TMS-evoked neural responses. These findings identify discomfort-related activity as an important confounding factor in TMS studies and highlight the need to routinely assess TMS-induced discomfort and consider its potential influence when estimating TMS-evoked neural effects, thereby improving the interpretability and rigor of TMS research and therapeutic applications.

item.title: Pathogenic mechanism of exacerbated brain atrophy in Alzheimer's disease exhibiting co-pathology of TDP-43.
item.description:
Brain research
While most Alzheimer's disease (AD) which is associated with Limbic Predominant Age-related TDP-43 Encephalopathy (LATE) exhibits accelerated brain atrophy, the pathogenic mechanism remains undefined. In this Perspective, we offer a feed-forward model of TDP-43 dysfunction linked to tauopathy that underpins such exacerbated neuron loss in AD with the co-pathology of TDP-43. Since TDP-43 dysfunction may be initiated in some central neurons of the aging human brain, we modeled this aspect of the human pathophysiology by ablating the gene encoding TDP-43 in excitatory neurons of the mouse forebrain and crossbred them to a tau-seeding mouse model. We found that such selective loss of TDP-43 function facilitated the pathological conversion of endogenous tau to accelerate tauopathy, resulting in exacerbated neuron loss. Since endogenous tau is a substrate of caspases, our finding that TDP-43 dysfunction activated caspase 3 could account at least in part for such an impact on tauopathy. Surprisingly, in our tau-seeding mouse model with deposition of Ab plaques, TDP-43 proteinopathy occurred during late-stage of disease, the emergence of which is dependent on tauopathy. We propose a novel mouse model of AD with the co-pathology of TDP-43 and discuss the potential use of such model to clarify disease mechanisms, disclose novel targets, and to test therapeutic strategies designed to attenuate proteinopathies of tau and TDP-43.

item.title: MoCA deficits and white matter in Huntington's disease.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
This study explored the relationship between the Montreal Cognitive Assessment's (MoCA) subdomains and white matter changes in Huntington's disease (HD). Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were measured using Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) in 22 early-stage symptomatic HD patients and 20 healthy controls. Tract-Based Spatial Statistics was used to compare the two groups and to correlate patients' FA and MD values with their performance on MoCA subdomains. Among all MoCA subdomains, only visuospatial performance was associated with white matter integrity in the corpus callosum, corona radiata, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, supporting the utility of identifying regional imaging correlates of specific cognitive performance through the combination of DTI analysis and brief screening tools in early-stage patients.

item.title: Limited white matter diffusion alterations after olfactory groove meningioma resection.
item.description:
Journal of neuro-oncology
Despite successful surgical resection, many patients with skull base meningiomas experience persistent neurological and neuropsychological deficits. Diffusion tensor imaging enables characterization of white matter microstructural integrity, yet longitudinal studies remain scarce. This study examined longitudinal white matter tract changes in patients with olfactory groove meningiomas. This prospective study included 35 patients with olfactory groove meningiomas who underwent comprehensive preoperative and long-term postoperative (n = 25, ≥ 6 months) clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging assessments, along with 20 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Diffusion tensor imaging was acquired on a 3T scanner, and 11 white matter tracts were reconstructed in each participant. Linear mixed models compared diffusion metrics across groups. Multivariable regression, cluster analysis, and ROC analysis identified predictors of white matter recovery. Preoperatively, patients showed widespread microstructural alterations in the uncinate fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, anterior thalamic radiation, and forceps minor. Only the left uncinate fasciculus showed significant postoperative increase in axial diffusivity (p = 0.003), though values remained below those of healthy controls. Peritumoral edema volume was the strongest predictor of these alterations, explaining approximately 50% of variance (R² = 0.49-0.60, p < 0.001). Edema volume > 41,145 mm³ discriminated the cluster with little or no postoperative diffusion change (AUC = 0.93). Cluster analysis of postoperative changes in axial diffusivity identified two patterns: little or no change in 24% of patients (n = 6) and moderate change in 76% (n = 19). No significant correlations were found between tract-specific changes and clinical outcomes. Postoperative alterations in white matter diffusion metrics is limited and primarily determined by preoperative edema burden. Peritumoral edema may cause irreversible microstructural damage despite successful surgery, highlighting the importance of edema management. The dissociation between structural and functional outcomes underscores the need for multimodal approaches to understand postoperative recovery.

item.title: Consciousness, complexity, and clinical implications.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Consciousness remains one of science's most challenging problems because it cannot be exhaustively characterized as a single function, computation, or behavior; it also refers to the presence and organization of subjective experience. This position paper integrates clinical neurology, neurophysiology, psychiatry, psychoanalysis, embodied cognition, moral neuroscience, theoretical physics, philosophy of mind, and neurotechnology. We argue that, despite major advances in identifying neural correlates, computational models, and behavioral markers, contemporary consciousness research has not resolved the explanatory gap between objective description and subjective experience. We propose that claims about consciousness at neurophysiological, embodied, cognitive, social, and ontological levels should be coordinated through explicit cross-level constraints rather than merged into a single unitary theory. These domains have different evidential roles and are not all constituents of consciousness. Perturbational measures of cortical complexity, including the Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) and its state-transition variant (PCIst), support assessment of preserved conscious capacity in studied human populations. They do not independently determine a clinical diagnosis or phenomenal content. Evidence from aphasia, sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness also demonstrates dissociations among language, wakefulness, behavioral responsiveness, and conscious experience. Perspectives from embodied simulation, mind-object identity, quantum information, and the philosophy of physics are treated here as heuristic stress tests rather than as mechanistic accounts; they keep open foundational questions concerning subjectivity, representation, and the role of the observer. We advocate constrained pluralism, a methodological framework in which consciousness is conceptualized as an integrated, embodied, relational, and temporally extended process. Such an approach provides a coherent foundation for future research while strengthening the dialogue between neuroscience, clinical practice, philosophy, and neuroethics.

item.title: Krüppel regulates cell cycle exit and limits adult neurogenesis of mushroom body neural progenitors in Drosophila.
item.description:
eLife
Neural progenitors typically exit the cell cycle during development, limiting adult neurogenesis. Here, we identify Krüppel (Kr) as a regulator of cell cycle exit and elimination of mushroom body neuroblasts (MBNBs) in Drosophila . Neuroblast (NB)-specific Kr RNAi and the Irregular facet (KrIf-1 ) mutation prolong MBNB lifespan and enable continued adult neurogenesis. Despite low post-embryonic expression, pupal stage-specific Kr depletion or misexpression causes MBNB retention, revealing a role distinct from its established embryonic function. Persistent MBNBs retain the early temporal factor IGF2 mRNA-binding protein (Imp) and fail to fully induce the late temporal factors Syncrip (Syp) and Eip93F (E93). Imp co-depletion suppresses MBNB retention following Kr depletion, identifying Imp as a key downstream effector. Krüppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1), a hormone-responsive transcription factor, functionally antagonises Kr by suppressing E93 expression. Kr-h1 knockdown partially rescues MBNB retention caused by Kr depletion, whereas its overexpression drives tumour-like NB overgrowth. Together, these findings identify Kr as a lineage-specific regulator coordinating the Imp/Syp transition and E93 expression to promote timely MBNB termination. This work reveals how temporal regulators control neural progenitor lifespan and restrict adult neurogenesis, linking intrinsic developmental programmes with hormone-responsive pathways in the Drosophila brain.

item.title: A dynamical mechanism for opposing cortical gradients in resting-state functional and stimulation-derived effective connectomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and stimulation-derived effective connectivity (EC) offer complementary views of cortical interactions, yet how cortical dynamics shape their relationship within a shared anatomical network remains unclear. Using group-level resting-state fMRI and intracranial electrical stimulation data from large-scale human cohorts, we find that regional mean response to electrical stimulation is negatively correlated with its mean FC (r=-0.568), with the two measures exhibiting opposing trends along the cortical hierarchy. To account for this divergence, we develop a differentiable whole-cortex mean-field model with independently trainable regional parameters, fitted to EC and FC through two-stage EC--FC training using gradient-based optimization. The optimized model reproduces EC (r=0.733) and FC (r=0.726) connectomes and their opposing regional signatures. Without prescribing a hierarchical parameter map, training yields a consistent organization in which recurrent strength and intrinsic noise increase from sensory to association cortex, whereas background input decreases. Linearization based analytical argument and parameter perturbation experiments further suggest how this organization can enhance evoked responsiveness while weakening resting-state correlations along the cortical hierarchy. Together, these findings link opposing connectome signatures, cortical hierarchy and emergent regional parameter organization, while providing a deep-learning-enabled, multimodal modelling framework for investigating cortical dynamics.

item.title: Evidence supporting resting-state power spectrum exponent as a non-invasive measure of neural-circuit excitation:inhibition balance in children with and without autism
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Introduction: An ongoing neural circuit excitation (E) and inhibition (I) imbalance is thought to be a major contributor to clinical conditions such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Current methods for directly measuring E:I dynamics require invasive procedures that are difficult to perform in non-human animals and nearly impossible in humans. A non-invasive measure of E:I balance is of great interest as a diagnostic as well as therapeutic marker, and as a means of studying relevant pathological and intervention mechanisms. Scientists have recently developed a computational model to show that, using resting-state (RS) MEG or EEG recordings, the E:I balance can be estimated from the power law exponent (slope) of the electrophysiological power spectrum. In their model, the RS power spectrum exponent is hypothesized to reflect the integration of synaptic currents in the brain, an index of E:I balance driven largely by excitatory (glutamate, Glu) and inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA) neurotransmitter levels. Glu and GABA are the principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain, together shaping the balance between neural circuit excitation and inhibition. The present study shows that parietal-occipital neurochemistry as a predictor of the parietal-occipital RS exponent is driven by inhibitory neurotransmitter levels in typically developing (TD) children but not in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Methods: Midline parietal-occipital RS power spectra (MEG) and Glu and GABA+ concentration (MRS) were obtained from 129 children (TD N = 84, ASD N = 45) 10.2 to 17.9 years old, with follow-up measures in a subset of the children providing 148 MEG and MRS datasets. Analyses focused on RS neural function and Glu and GABA+ concentration in parietal-occipital cortex. Results: t-tests showed no group differences between the parietal-occipital exponent, Glu, GABA+, or Glu/GABA+ ratio measures (ps > 0.21). In the full sample, older age was marginally associated with a lower exponent (p = 0.07), and older age associated with lower Glu concentration (p < 0.05). Age and GABA concentration or Glu/GABA+ associations were not observed (p > 0.05). There was no main effect of Glu or a Glu x group interaction with the exponent (ps > 0.14). Simple effect analyses of interactions for GABA+ (p < 0.05) and ratio (p<0.05) showed a GABA+ and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.40) and a ratio and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.83). Discussion: The brain chemistry and RS exponent associations suggest that a simple method for estimating E:I ratio reduces a major hurdle in understanding a currently difficult-to-measure, yet fundamental aspect of neural computation that has been proposed as central to clinical conditions such as ASD, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. Present findings indicate that the contribution of local brain chemistry to neural-circuit E:I balance differs for older children with and without ASD, with GABA inhibition presenting the more promising contributor to the E:I balance in TD children. Findings have the potential for high impact, including identifying neural markers for use in tracking treatment response

item.title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Neurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. Methods: We collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. Results: We replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

item.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

item.title: Age and bilingual language experience are associated with large-scale functional network reorganization
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Aging is associated with changes in large-scale functional brain organization, such as reductions in network segregation, which have been interpreted as a feature of age-related neural dedifferentiation. However, functional network organization may may also reflect accumulated life experiences. Bilingualism, in particular, has been linked to experience-dependent variation in cognitive and neural systems supporting language processing and executive control. Whether bilingualism is associated with network segregation across adulthood, and how these associations vary with language experience, remains unclear. To address this question, the present multisite study examines resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) among the Language network, the Default Mode (DMN), and the Multiple Demand (MD) (which support language processing, internally directed cognition, and domain-general cognitive control, respectively). The sample comprised N= 605 adults spanning younger to older adulthood, drawn from eight independent datasets across four sociolinguistic contexts. Older age was associated with less segregation across all three network pairs. Notably, bilingual adults showed greater Language–DMN, Language–MD, and DMN–MD segregation than monolingual adults. Immersion-defined contrasts further revealed variation across linguistic environments such that both immersed and non-immersed bilinguals showed greater DMN-MD segregation than monolinguals, while greater Language–MD segregation was observed primarily in immersed bilinguals compared to monolinguals. In contrast, continuous measures of bilingual experience were not significantly associated with segregation and did not modulate age-related differences. Together, these findings highlight age-related reductions in network segregation and demonstrate that bilingual language experience is associated with systemic differences in large-scale functional network organization across adulthood.
